catalog_quote: The Naxi language, spoken in Yunnan, China, has H, M and L tones, plus a marginal Rising tone. This is an ‘easy’ tone system. Tones are lexically attached to syllables and there are extremely few processes of tonal change [20]. Phonetically, the tones are readily identifiable; there are no oppositions in the language that could complicate their production and perception, such as vowel quantity [24], phonation types, distinctive stress, or glottalized consonants [6]. Syllable structure is (C)(G)V+Tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Naxi is a level-tone language with one lexical tone (H, M, L, marginal rising) per (C)(G)V syllable; the language has no distinctive (lexical) stress. The same author states in French (Michaud 2003, MSLP XIII, postprint p.15-16) that Naxi is a 'langue sans accent lexical' in which every syllable has its own tone, prominence being realised by local intonational means.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress (no word stress posited).
new_statements.exceptions: None at word level. Phrase-level prominence phenomena described elsewhere by Michaud (2005 thesis, 2006 Speech Prosody, 2006 LTBA, 2007 JIPA): emphatic stress (accent d'insistance) and an intonational 'intensive' H tone; intonation-group-final lengthening with F0 lowering; grammatical words prosodically weaker/lower than lexical words and subject to syllable reduction; within a disyllable the second syllable tends to be realised at lower F0 (word-level declination), described as allotonic, not accentual.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns the lexical/word level (absence of distinctive stress) for Western (Lijiang-plain) Naxi; recordings made in Lijiang with four native speakers (F2, M5, M7, M9), the same consultants as Michaud's 2005 thesis (main fieldwork village /ɑ̄ ʂə˞̀/, Wenhua, Jinshan township, c. 20 km NE of Lijiang town). Prominence and lengthening effects reported by the author are intonational (phrase/utterance level, carrier-sentence citation forms).
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand statements are by Alexis Michaud on Western Naxi of the Lijiang plain (naxi1245 proper; Glottolog 'Lijiang' dialect area): main fieldwork village /ɑ̄ ʂə˞̀/ (冷不罗, Wenhua 文化 administrative village, Jinshan 金山 township, c. 20 km NE of Lijiang town) plus Lijiang-town speakers; the ICPhS 2015 recordings were made in Lijiang with speakers F2, M5, M7, M9. Not to be confused with Yongning Na / Narua (yong1270) or Laze, sister Naish languages treated in Michaud 2017 and in the ECLL article; the Pianding dialect paper (Michaud & He Likun 2015) describes an eastern-area Naxi variety and is silent on stress.

tone_statements.quote: Le système tonal du na de Lijiang, relativement simple, comprend trois tons ponctuels : Haut, Moyen, Bas, transcrits par les diacritiques / ́/, / ̄/, / ̀/. A Fèng Kē, il existe un ton lexical supplémentaire : un contour montant. Dans les deux dialectes, des tons modulés apparaissent lors de l’ellipse d’une syllabe, dont seul demeure le ton, qui s’associe alors à la syllabe qui précède ... Aucun interdit ne pèse sur les séquences tonales : toute la combinatoire est attestée, sur les mots disyllabiques (Haut + Haut, Bas + Haut, Moyen + Bas, etc.) comme dans le fil de l’énoncé.
tone_statements.translation: The tone system of Lijiang Na, relatively simple, comprises three level tones: High, Mid, Low, transcribed by the diacritics / ́/, / ̄/, / ̀/. At Feng Ke there is an additional lexical tone: a rising contour. In both dialects, contour tones appear upon elision of a syllable of which only the tone remains, which then associates to the preceding syllable ... No restriction bears on tonal sequences: all combinations are attested, on disyllabic words (High + High, Low + High, Mid + Low, etc.) as in running speech.
tone_statements.summary: Lijiang Naxi: three level tones H, M, L, one per syllable; rising tone rare in lexicon (lexical in Feng Ke); reduplication AA: L>M+L, H>H+M, M unchanged; F0/EGG study of 8 speakers; nothing on stress.

To me, it is equally clear (i) that the tone system of Na and Naxi is based on three level tones: H, M, and L, and that contours observed in these two languages are to be analyzed as sequences of levels

tone_statements.quote: 次恩丁纳西语单音节词上表现为三种调类。其发音为低[˩，11]、中[˧，33]、高升[˧˥，35]。进行音位归纳时，可以将高升调分析为一个简单的高调。这三种调类跟丽江坝其它方言（如笔者所调查过的古城区文化乡冷不罗村方言⑥，下文简称作“冷不罗纳西语”）有很直接的对应关系：见表 1。[…] 表 1 表明：次恩丁纳西语的调类少于丽江大研镇、冷不罗等地点的纳西语。后者方言的第四个调类（升调）是一个创新，起创一些语法作用，在词汇里（除借词外）很罕见⑦。这方面，次恩丁比起丽江坝有四个调类的方言更保守。[…] 次恩丁纳西语没有多少变调现象，这一点接近丽江坝不同方言如大研镇、冷不罗等等
tone_statements.translation: On monosyllabic words Ciending Naxi shows three tone categories, pronounced Low [11], Mid [33] and high-rising [35]. In the phonemic analysis the high-rising tone can be treated as a simple High tone. These three categories correspond very directly to those of the other dialects of the Lijiang plain (e.g. the Lengbuluo dialect of Wenhua township, surveyed by the author): see Table 1. [...] Table 1 shows that Ciending Naxi has fewer tone categories than the Naxi of Dayan (Lijiang), Lengbuluo etc. The fourth category of the latter dialects (the rising tone) is an innovation; it has some grammatical functions and is very rare in the vocabulary (loanwords apart). In this respect Ciending is more conservative than the four-category dialects of the Lijiang plain. [...] Ciending Naxi has few tone-change (sandhi) phenomena, like the Lijiang-plain dialects such as Dayan and Lengbuluo.

tone_statements.translation: Naxi belongs to the Yi branch of Tibeto-Burman, Sino-Tibetan, and is a typical tone language... The overall result for the eight speakers can be summarised as high level 55, mid level 33, mid falling 31 and low rising 13. ... tone_statements.translation: Table 1. The four-way tonal contrast of Pianding Naxi on monosyllables. Tone description: high level, mid level, low level, rising; letter labels (Michaud & He 2015) H M L MH; letter labels (this paper) H M L R; Naxi examples tʰɑ˥ tʰɑ˧ tʰɑ˩ tʰɑ˩˦ ... tone_statements.quote: Naxi has four phonemic tones, three level and one rising. The pitch of these four tones is /55/ for the high-level, /33/ for the mid-level, /11/ for the low level and /13/ for the rising. The phonetic shape of these four tones actually varies quite a bit. The high tone is sometimes articulated as [454], the mid tone sounds like [42], and the low tone most often is articulated with a slight fall [21] or [31]. ... The rising tone is extremely rare in Naxi words, being almost exclusively reserved for Chinese borrowed words.

tone_statements.summary: Four tones 55/33/11(~21)/13; rising rare, mostly loans; minimal sets tHA/xO/nA x4; limited word-internal sandhi (21+21>33+21, 55+55>55+33); floating H (fn.15); stress equal-weighted, study limited.

tone_statements.quote: This study shows that although Bōwān Naxi, a Western variety, has only four surface tones, it in fact operates with five underlying tone categories, among which two contrastive mid tones, termed Ma and Mb , are neutralized in monosyllabic verbs but exhibit distinct tonal patterns in multi-syllabic morphological contexts. Tonal behaviors of the 5 categories reveal that Ma is underlyingly associated with a floating high tone (/M#H/) while Mb is underlyingly toneless. ... the 4 surface tones: High Level (/55 /), Mid Level (/33 /), Low Level (/21 /), and Mid Rising (/24 /).

tone_statements.summary: Bowan W. Naxi: 4 surface tones H 55, M 33, L 21, Rising 24 (= LH sequence); 5 underlying verb categories /H, M#H, ∅, L, LH/ (Mb toneless); floating H docks on toneless affixes; nothing said on stress.

tone_statements.translation: Fengke tones comprise three level tones and one low-mid rising tone, namely high level (55), mid level (33), low level (11), low-mid rising (13), see Table 1; among the 2,500 common words of Fengke these three level tones account for 50.12%, 59.72%, 43.08% of the total respectively, occurring relatively frequently, whereas the low-mid rising tone (13) occurs relatively rarely, in 22.6% ... Hence the low-mid rising tone mostly occurs in disyllabic native words and Chinese loanwords of Fengke, rarely in monosyllabic native words. ... From the tone plot in Fig. 1 it can be seen that Fengke belongs to the three-level-tone dialects, with only one rising tone

tone.translation: On monosyllabic words Ciending Naxi shows three tone categories, pronounced Low [11], Mid [33] and high-rising [35]. tone.quote: The prosody of Naxi, a Tibeto-Burman language spoken in China, looks very straightforward: each syllable carries a High (˥), Mid (˧), or Low (˩) tone. Some morphemes can delete, leaving a floating tone which causes a preceding Low or Mid tone to become Rising. ... 3. /HH/ surfaces as [H] ... 4. /MH/ and /LH/ surface as one and the same [Rising] contour tone.
